Class Config

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.config.Config
public final class Config extends Object
Everything tunable without a rebuild. The mod writes this to swordai/config.json; when configVersion in the file is older than CURRENT_VERSION the file is backed up and regenerated, so new defaults shipped in a jar are never shadowed by a stale file.

    stages

    stepBackRule
    Against an opponent that answers its hits while its sword is on the way back (twice within five seconds), it walks backwards out of that opponent's reach after each hit of its own until its sword is nearly back; see StepBack.
    boolean
    straightInRule
    With the opponent in view and out of reach, the strafe keys are let go of, so that it runs straight in instead of going round in a circle; see StraightIn.

    On someone's server, how many ticks more it waits once the weapon is all the way back.

    The least charge the weapon must have for the network to be given the attack key at all; see SwingGate.
    float

    The same on someone's server, where it is at least this: the weapon all the way back, which is one tick more (thirteen after the last swing).

    tacticEntropy
    Its entropy bonus: keeps it trying every way now and then.
    float
    tacticLr
    The tactics model's learning rate (its own optimiser; the acting network's does not move it).
    boolean
    tacticModel
    The tactics model (rl.TacticNet): a network of its own chooses every half second how to fight (in and combo, crit back, space at the edge of the reach and crit back, or back off after a hit; rl.Tactic), which turns counterCritRule, edgeHoldRule and stepBackRule on and off in their place, and is handed to the acting network as an input.
    boolean
    tacticOnEvents
    The tactics model also chooses again right after a hit either way, a swing of the opponent's and a jump of the opponent's (at the least rl.Tactic.LEAST ticks after its last choice), not only every half second; see rl.Tactic.Clock.
    float
    tacticPriorWeight
    How firmly the tactics model is held near the plan it starts with (a KL to it on every choice, as the acting network is held near the installed one), 0 for not at all.
    boolean
    taskAdvantageNorm
    Normalise the advantages of each kind of fight on their own in an update, instead of all together (the point of PopArt, Hessel et al.
    boolean

    Every fight against a scripted opponent written down tick by tick to swordai/traces, for reading how fights are lost.
    int
    trainerThreads
    Trainer threads; 0 picks a value from the CPU count.
    float
    trainSpeed
    How many times normal speed /swordai train runs the game at (1 = real time).
    float
    uppercutChance
    The share of the hits of a combo of its own, from the third on, that an uppercut follows: a running jump and the sprint hit made on the way up; see JumpIn.
    boolean
    useFovea
     
    boolean
    usePeriphery
     
    int
    visionFov
    Field of view of the picture the network gets; never wider than fov.
    boolean
    watchStyles
    In /swordai fight, how the opponent fights is counted and kept in swordai/people/<name>.json (a few hundred bytes a player), and training fights scripted opponents made from those it has lost to or nearly; see PersonStyle and StageSpec.peopleShare.
    boolean
    whiffGuard
    No swing at an opponent plainly out of reach (read off its height on screen), or not on the screen at all: such a swing hits nothing, starts the sword over and hands the opponent a free hit.

    • visionFov

      public int visionFov
      Field of view of the picture the network gets; never wider than fov. When it is narrower, the network is handed the middle of each frame, which is exactly the narrower view. It has to be the field of view the network was trained with: /swordai fov sets it, and it is kept when a new version rewrites this file.

    • trainSpeed

      public float trainSpeed
      How many times normal speed /swordai train runs the game at (1 = real time). Above 1 the game window is made small, so that it can draw a fresh frame for every one of the shorter ticks, and the speed comes down by itself if the computer does not keep up. /swordai speed sets it.

    • speedWindowRows

      public int speedWindowRows
      Training faster than real time: the height of the picture the small window draws, in rows. 0 is the least the AI's picture needs (270 rows); set it higher for a window that is easier to read.

    • headlessSpeed

      public float headlessSpeed
      /swordai train headless: the most times normal speed the world may run at. It settles on what the computer manages, which is usually less.

    • botName

      public String botName
      The name of the fake player the AI fights (and that you fight in /swordai spar). A fake player gets the skin of the Minecraft account of that name, if there is one and the game can look it up. /swordai name sets it.

    • showOpponentSkin

      public boolean showOpponentSkin
      While the AI plays on the screen: show the opponent with its own skin, armour and name tag instead of the blue and green figure. The AI still gets the blue and green picture; it is drawn first, in a pass of its own, and then the world is drawn again for the player. That is two pictures per frame, so about half the frames a second. /swordai skin sets it.

    • agentName

      public String agentName
      Training without the screen: the name of the fake player that is the AI's own body.

    • trainerThreads

      public int trainerThreads
      Trainer threads; 0 picks a value from the CPU count.

    • aimResponse

      public float aimResponse
      How quickly the camera takes up the turning speed the agent asks for: the share of the gap closed each tick. 1 would be instant (and twitchy); lower is smoother and slower to react.

    • playTemperature

      public float playTemperature
      How /swordai play, fight and spar pick from the network's choices. At 1 they pick exactly as training does, so what plays is what was trained and watched. Below 1 the network commits to its favourite choice more often, which looks steadier but changes how it plays: things it does only now and then on purpose, like letting go of W for one tick to get its sprint hit back, become rare.

    • fightMixAssist

      public boolean fightMixAssist
      /swordai fight and /swordai spar with a policy that has not passed the mix-up stage yet: when set, its strafe direction and hit timing are varied for it by rule. Off by default, so that what fights is exactly the network that was trained.

    • learnFromPeople

      public boolean learnFromPeople
      /swordai fight and /swordai spar also teach the network: it learns from those fights against people with the rewards of the stage it is in. They never count towards passing a stage. Off unless /swordai learn on says otherwise.

      (On by default from 0.11.0 to 0.13.3. What that did to a trained network was measured in 0.13.2: nine updates from sparring and from fights on a server, each from a minute of fighting or less and each moving the network three to seven times as far as a training update does, the last four on fights the critic could make nothing of. Early swings went from one in twenty to seven in ten and sprint hits from nine in ten to one in ten.)

    • safeLearn

      public boolean safeLearn
      With learnFromPeople on, how /swordai fight learns: safely. The proven network (the trained one) and a copy that learns take turns, a fight each; the copy learns from its own fights with small, cautious updates, and takes the proven one's place only when it has done better (damage dealt minus taken a minute) over enough fights of each, or is thrown away when it does worse; see SafeLearn. The proven network is never changed otherwise. Since 19 October. False learns as up to 0.15.1: the network itself, from every fight.

    • silWeight

      public float silWeight
      Self-imitation learning (Oh et al., 2018; SilBuffer): after each update, the steps that went far better than the critic expected are learned from again, for as long as they still do. The weight of that on the actor; 0 is off. Since 20 October: the rare wins over an opponent it mostly loses to were learned from once and gone.

    • silValueWeight

      public float silValueWeight
      The same on the critic, which is raised towards those returns.

    • silBatches

      public int silBatches
      Minibatches of self-imitation after each update.

    • silCapacity

      public int silCapacity
      Steps kept to be imitated, the most recent.

    • silClip

      public float silClip
      The most a step's lead over what was expected counts for.

    • silKeepZ

      public float silKeepZ
      A step is kept when its advantage stands this many standard deviations above its update's mean.

    • demoWeight

      public float demoWeight
      Learning from the user's own fights, recorded with /swordai demo (DemoFile; the user, 22 October): after each update, demoBatches minibatches of the recorded steps where the person did better than the critic expects of the network are imitated with this weight, the way silWeight imitates its own best steps. 0 is off. The fights are read when training starts.

    • demoBatches

      public int demoBatches

    • demoValueWeight

      public float demoValueWeight
      The same on the critic. 0: the critic stays the network's own and is not raised towards a person's returns.

    • demoMaxSteps

      public int demoMaxSteps
      At most this many recorded steps are read, the newest fights first; a step is about 5 KB in memory.

    • demoWindowTicks

      public int demoWindowTicks
      A recorded step is learned from only if the reward of the next this-many ticks, its own included, adds up to more than nothing: the stretch after it went the person's way. 0: every step (the critic's comparison alone decides). The user, 23 October: the opponents are hard for them too, "some part are me losing and so it might learn the part that I lose".

    • demoWindowMin

      public float demoWindowMin
      What that stretch's reward has to come to, more than this. 0: ahead at all (an even trade, a hit for a hit, is not: being hit costs about 4, a hit brings about 2). 3.5: a critical hit (4 to 5) or two clean hits, the user's crit combos (23 October: "only some part where I manage get into a crit combo").

    • anchorWeight

      public float anchorWeight
      Kickstarting (Schmitt et al., 2018; Wołczyk et al., 2024, "Fine-tuning reinforcement learning models is secretly a forgetting mitigation problem"): the weight of KL(anchor || network) on the actor, on the states of every update, where the anchor is the network in swordai/anchor.bin (the one installed) and is never trained. Updates still move the network where the advantage says, but each step away from what the anchor does costs, so what it was good at is not walked away from. 0 is off; the drift from the anchor is logged whenever the file is there. Since 20 October: every network trained on from the installed one measured worse than it within hours.

    • anchorBoostWeight

      public float anchorBoostWeight
      The anchor's weight on the steps of the kinds of fight listed in anchorBoostTasks (their places in Trainer.episodeTask), when above 0; the rest keep anchorWeight. Targeted distillation (Distral, Teh et al. 2017): on 21 October the installed network beat everything trained since against the spacer, fight by fight on the same 118 fights, while the newer networks did a little better against the rest; so where the spacer is fought the network is held to the installed one firmly, and elsewhere it keeps what it learned.

    • anchorGainWeight

      public float anchorGainWeight
      At 0 or above: on a step whose action did better than the critic expected (advantage above 0), the anchor's weight is at most this. The anchor then holds the network back where it does worse than expected and not where it finds something better: a floor, not a ceiling. Below 0, off: the anchor pulls the same on every step. Since 21 October evening (suggested in a review the user passed on).

    • anchorBoostTasks

      public int[] anchorBoostTasks

    • evalSeed

      public int evalSeed
      Paired evaluation (common random numbers): not 0, every fight is set up from this number and its place in the run (which stage, which opponent and how it is made, where both start, and the arena's and the bot's own random choices), so two networks measured with the same number meet the same fights in the same order and the difference between them is not the luck of the draw. For frozen measurements only; 0 (training) draws every fight afresh. Since 20 October: the same network measured +88 and -9 net against the spacer in two seven-minute runs.

    • pairedBase

      public String pairedBase
      With evalSeed: every fight is fought twice in the same run, once by this network (A) and once by the network saved here (B: a run folder or a checkpoint file), from the same seed, the order turning from one pair to the next; see PairedEval. Both then share the run's luck (its connection, its timing, the machine), which two separate runs did not (20 to 23 October: the same network measured -15 and +92 on the same fights in two runs). "" for none. Gemini's review, 23 October (rank 6).

    • pairedBaseSettings

      public String pairedBaseSettings
      The settings B fights with, as "key=value key=value" (plain fields only), A's own put back for its fights: the installed network is measured without the coach counters, say "keepWithin=0 jumpAtReadyOnlyFleeing=false". A B saved without a tactics model plays with none.

    • actorVecWide

      public int actorVecWide
      The size of the networks, grown on 21 October 2026 (the user: "it might be too small"). Up to then the actor decided everything from one layer of 128 over 64 units of the vector input (6.7k of its 153k weights; the rest read the two pictures), and the critic was 132-128-128-1 and explained under half of the returns. Every part added starts out computing nothing, so a network saved before loads and plays exactly as it did, and grows from there:
      • actorVecWide more units reading the vector input straight into the trunk;
      • actorBlocks residual blocks of actorBlockWidth between the trunk and the heads, as SimBa (Lee et al., ICLR 2025) scales RL networks: layer norm, a skip path, the block's output starting at zero (see ResBlock);
      • for the critic, which kind of fight it is (criticTask, never shown to the actor) and criticBlocks blocks of its own.
      A network saved with more parts than these settings make does not load: set them back to what it was trained with.

    • actorBlocks

      public int actorBlocks

    • actorBlockWidth

      public int actorBlockWidth

    • criticTask

      public boolean criticTask

    • criticBlocks

      public int criticBlocks

    • criticBlockWidth

      public int criticBlockWidth

    • taskAdvantageNorm

      public boolean taskAdvantageNorm
      Normalise the advantages of each kind of fight on their own in an update, instead of all together (the point of PopArt, Hessel et al. AAAI 2019); see Ppo.setTaskNormalisation.

    • replayLostShare

      public float replayLostShare
      In training, the share of the fights against a stage's scripted opponents that are fights it lost before, set up exactly as they were, until each has been won twice in a row; see LostCases. Since 19 October: a fight it still loses is very likely the one a person finds.

    • replayByPotential

      public boolean replayByPotential
      Lost fights are replayed by how much they have to teach (prioritised level replay, the mean |GAE| of their last fighting) instead of by how badly they were lost; see LostCases.byPotential.

    • mutateShare

      public float mutateShare
      Of the scripted fights that are not replays, the share made from a kept fight (lost, or lately beaten) changed a little: the edge of what it can do, explored around (ACCEL). 0 is off.

    • answerSpareBacking

      public boolean answerSpareBacking
      The answer rule owes no swing to an opponent backing straight out after a single hit (the spacer's crit, S): the sword is kept for its next jump in, which the meet rule hits out of the air. A combo (the second hit in a row) is always answered. See AnswerRule.opponentBacking.

    • swingMinCharge

      public float swingMinCharge
      The least charge the weapon must have for the network to be given the attack key at all; see SwingGate. Zero leaves every swing to the network, as up to 0.13.3. Eleven ticks after the last swing since 18 October (SwingGate.EARLY_CHARGE); twelve before.

    • ruleSwingCharge

      public float ruleSwingCharge
      The least charge for a swing a rule makes for it (the answer it owes, the run at an opponent on its way up): the sword all the way back, twelve ticks after the last swing. Whether to swing a tick sooner is the network's to learn, not a rule's.

    • swingMinChargeOnline

      public float swingMinChargeOnline
      The same on someone's server, where it is at least this: the weapon all the way back, which is one tick more (thirteen after the last swing). A server counts the time between two swings in its own ticks, from when they reach it. If two of them arrive a tick or two closer together than they were made, or the server is running slow, a swing made the moment the weapon was back on the fighter's own screen is one made too early as the server counts it: no knockback, no critical hit, less damage. The tick in hand is what keeps that from happening.

      Twelve ticks (0.96) from 18 October, back to thirteen (1.0, as in 0.14.0) the same evening: at 105 ms the user saw weak hits again. Two ticks in hand, as 0.14.0 had, and no weak hit is worth the tick of rhythm.

    • ruleSwingChargeOnline

      public float ruleSwingChargeOnline
      The same for the swings a rule makes, on someone's server: thirteen ticks, as every swing was up to 18 October. The network's own may come a tick sooner (swingMinChargeOnline, twelve ticks: on a connection that brings two swings a tick closer together the server counts eleven, 0.92, which is still more than the nine tenths it asks for).

    • swingExtraTicksOnline

      public int swingExtraTicksOnline
      On someone's server, how many ticks more it waits once the weapon is all the way back. None unless a server still makes weak hits of its swings: the result of a fight says how many of its swings were early as its own game counted them, and if that is none and the hits are weak all the same, the server is counting shorter, and each tick here is one more in hand. Each also costs a thirteenth of its hits.

    • answerRule

      public boolean answerRule
      Hit, and not yet having hit back, it swings as soon as its sword is back and the opponent is under its crosshair and near enough; see AnswerRule. A rule, in training and in every fight, so that it never takes a combo without swinging back where a swing was there to be made. False leaves that to the network, as up to the first runs of 0.14.0.

    • answerNudge

      public float answerNudge
      Not 0: the answer rule pushes instead of pressing. Where it would swing for the fighter, this is added to the network's swing logit, and where it would hold the swing back, taken off; the network's own choice is then what is done and what is learned from (Residual Policy Learning, Silver et al. 2018). Up to 21 October the rule pressed the key itself and took the attack head out of the step it decided, about 78 swings in 100: the network never learned when to swing right after being hit, the very moment spacing is decided in (a rule that overrides the agent without telling it is a "shield", Alshiekh et al. AAAI 2018, and such shields hold learning back). 0 keeps the rule pressing, as before.

    • tacticModel

      public boolean tacticModel
      The tactics model (rl.TacticNet): a network of its own chooses every half second how to fight (in and combo, crit back, space at the edge of the reach and crit back, or back off after a hit; rl.Tactic), which turns counterCritRule, edgeHoldRule and stepBackRule on and off in their place, and is handed to the acting network as an input. It learns by PPO at its own pace from its own choices. The user's idea of 21 October: a decision model made only to choose the way to fight. A network trained with it must be played with it.

    • tacticLr

      public float tacticLr
      The tactics model's learning rate (its own optimiser; the acting network's does not move it).

    • tacticEntropy

      public float tacticEntropy
      Its entropy bonus: keeps it trying every way now and then.

    • tacticPriorWeight

      public float tacticPriorWeight
      How firmly the tactics model is held near the plan it starts with (a KL to it on every choice, as the acting network is held near the installed one), 0 for not at all. On 21 October, unheld, it went from crit back on 45% of its choices to 7% in two hours of training: crit back pays against the spacer and not against the jump-crit chaser and the whiffer, and without telling them apart it dropped it everywhere; the spacer went from +58 to -70 a minute.

    • tacticOnEvents

      public boolean tacticOnEvents
      The tactics model also chooses again right after a hit either way, a swing of the opponent's and a jump of the opponent's (at the least rl.Tactic.LEAST ticks after its last choice), not only every half second; see rl.Tactic.Clock.

    • opponentReader

      public boolean opponentReader
      The opponent reader (rl.OpponentReader; only with tacticModel): a small network reads the last 3.2 seconds of the fight into sixteen numbers, taught to name the kind of opponent, and hands them to the tactics model and the acting network. A network trained with it must be played with it.

    • critBridge

      public boolean critBridge
      The crit model (the jump key, and W/S, the sprint key and the swing in a jump) and the escape model (W/S just after a hit of a combo) read what the trunk has made of the fight (after the blocks, the tactic and the opponent reader) and the reader's numbers, not the vector input alone; see rl.ActorNet. Read-only: what they learn does not go back into the trunk. They start at zero, so a network plays exactly as before until it learns to use them. Gemini's audit, 23 October: the 32-unit crit model never knew which opponent it faced. A network trained with it must be played with it.

    • rhythmNet

      public boolean rhythmNet
      A memory of the last 3.2 seconds for the acting network: a causal temporal convolution over the opponent reader's window, into the trunk and the crit and escape models through weights that start at zero, learned from the policy's own gradient; see rl.RhythmNet. Only with the reader (opponentReader), whose window it reads. Gemini's review, 23 October, and the user: build it. A network trained with it must be played with it.

    • traceFights

      public boolean traceFights
      Every fight against a scripted opponent written down tick by tick to swordai/traces, for reading how fights are lost.

    • readerLr

      public float readerLr
      The reader's learning rate (its own optimiser).

    • readerBatches

      public int readerBatches
      Minibatches of 128 it learns from after each update, drawn from its memory of this many steps; see rl.OpponentReader.Memory.

    • readerMemory

      public int readerMemory

    • punishRule

      public boolean punishRule
      In the air, the swing that rule makes is kept for the way down and made as a critical hit, the punish crit; see AnswerRule.inTheAir. False makes it the moment the rule applies.

    • punishWaitOnGround

      public boolean punishWaitOnGround
      On the ground, the swing kept for the way down is kept for as long as the hit is fresh (a second), as up to 14 October; false keeps it on the tick of the hit only, and from the next tick on a swing that reaches is made. See AnswerRule.onTheGround.

    • hopRule

      public boolean hopRule
      A running jump, and another as it lands, at an opponent five blocks off or more that is not itself coming in at a run: it closes the distance faster than a run, and the hit at the end of the last one is a critical hit if the way down brings the opponent into reach; see JumpIn.approachHops. Hit in the air of such a jump, it leaves them alone for a while.

    • chaseRule

      public boolean chaseRule
      A running jump is made for it at an opponent it is running after and not catching, a few steps beyond its reach, and the hit on the way down is made a critical hit; see JumpIn.

    • chaseClosingMost

      public float chaseClosingMost
      That jump is made at an opponent the run is closing on by no more than this, in blocks a tick. 0.31: at any opponent that is not itself coming in, also one that holds its ground a step or two out of reach (a run closes on that one by 0.28). 0.15: only at one that is backing off or running. Hit in the air of such a jump, it does not make another for fifteen seconds either way.

    • faceRule

      public boolean faceRule
      A jump is made for it when the opponent is still in its face a few ticks after its hit, and the hit on the way down is a critical hit: against one that a hit does not send away; see JumpIn.

    • uppercutChance

      public float uppercutChance
      The share of the hits of a combo of its own, from the third on, that an uppercut follows: a running jump and the sprint hit made on the way up; see JumpIn. 0: never.

    • farRestRule

      public boolean farRestRule
      The camera is left alone while the opponent is far away and the crosshair is on it or all but on it; see FarRest.

    • lostRule

      public boolean lostRule
      With the opponent off the screen for three ticks, the camera turns to the side it was last seen on and comes level until it is found; see LostRule. Since 18 October.

    • straightInRule

      public boolean straightInRule
      With the opponent in view and out of reach, the strafe keys are let go of, so that it runs straight in instead of going round in a circle; see StraightIn. Since 18 October.

    • whiffGuard

      public boolean whiffGuard
      No swing at an opponent plainly out of reach (read off its height on screen), or not on the screen at all: such a swing hits nothing, starts the sword over and hands the opponent a free hit. See SwingGate.outOfReach. Since 18 October.

    • hardOpponents

      public boolean hardOpponents
      In training, the kinds of scripted opponent it has been losing rounds to come up more often, and the ones it nearly always beats less (prioritized fictitious self-play, as AlphaStar picked its opponents). Since 18 October; off unless set.

    • outsideShare

      public float outsideShare
      In training, this share of the scripted fights is against the outside bot: Carpet PvP's own fighter (a fork of Carpet whose fake players fight by themselves, https://modrinth.com/mod/carpet-pvp-practice), where the game runs on it instead of Carpet. An opponent that was not written here, at the levels in outsideLevels. Zero (off) unless set; without Carpet PvP in the game it never comes up. Since 18 October.

    • outsideLevels

      public String outsideLevels
      The levels the outside bot plays at, one drawn per fight: beginner, casual, average, skilled, expert.

    • recordRounds

      public boolean recordRounds
      Every round of /swordai fight is written to swordai/fights, tick by tick, with what likely decided it; the newest 200 are kept. See RoundRecorder. Since 18 October.

    • oldModelShare

      public float oldModelShare
      The share of the fights against copies of itself that are against the old model, where one is kept (swordai/old-model.bin, with the settings it played with in old-model-config.json). It plays as it did: its sword all the way back every time, the rules it had then. The user, 18 October: the old model "can be spaced", so a network that spaces it, finds the timing loophole and combos it has learned to choose its timing. Since 18 October.

    • punishInCombo

      public boolean punishInCombo
      Whether, being comboed, it still keeps its swing for the way down against an opponent it has made a punish crit on (the exception in AnswerRule.when). Off since 18 October: against the user's friend that was nearly every hit of a combo, a swing held in the air and made on the exact tick of the fall, time after time, and to the friend it looked like a trigger bot rather than a fighter. Being comboed it now swings back the moment it can; the swing kept for the way down is for the first hit of an exchange.

    • counterCritRule

      public boolean counterCritRule
      Crit back: with the opponent's sword on its way back (it has just swung, hit or miss) and its own sword nearly back, an opponent at the edge of the reach is jumped at and hit on the way down, a critical hit in the opponent's cooldown; see JumpIn.COUNTER. Since 19 October: players who space it crit it and sprint-hit it, and it never critted back. Off: in the frozen test of 19 October evening it cost more damage than it won with both networks tried (against the hard scripted opponents, damage dealt minus taken a minute -64 with it and -24 without; v19 -76 and -49).

    • meetWhenComing

      public boolean meetWhenComing
      An opponent jumping in for a crit is met (see MeetJump) also when it is the opponent alone that is coming, the fighter still being carried back by a hit: before 19 October only when the two were closing fast, which a hit taken a moment before ruled out on half the jumps.

    • dodgeJumpRule

      public boolean dodgeJumpRule
      An opponent jumping in at it while its own sword is not back (it cannot meet that jump with a hit): it holds S for that jump, so the crit comes down out of reach, and comes in again once its sword is back; see MeetJump.dodges. Since 19 October: on half the jumps made at it its sword was not back, and those were the crits it took. Off: in training it lost the spacer more rounds than before (49% won without it, 29% with it), half an hour each on 19 October.

    • keepWithin

      public float keepWithin
      The swing owed for a hit taken is kept for the fighter's way down (the punish crit, AnswerRule.inTheAir) only with the opponent nearer than this, as JumpIn.distance reads it; farther off it is made at once, while the opponent is still under the crosshair. 0: always kept, as before 22 October. From the fight traces of 22 October: thrown up by a hit at 2.6 blocks or more, the crit came on 28% of those swings against the spacer and 10% against the one that stands and hits, and against those two the swing was never made at all on 42% and 30% of the openings where its sword was spent and the fighter's back (the knockback carried the fighter out of reach while it waited). Nearer than 2.2 the crit came on 68 to 97% of them, against every kind.

    • jumpAtReadyOnlyFleeing

      public boolean jumpAtReadyOnlyFleeing
      The chase and the hop (JumpIn.CHASE, JumpIn.HOP) are only made at an opponent whose sword is not ready, or that is running away; never at one standing its ground with its sword ready. From the fight traces of 22 October: a running jump at a ready opponent that holds its ground is hit out of the air before it comes down (in the air the fighter's eye is higher and its reach to a grounded opponent shorter, and such an opponent hits whatever comes into its reach): the one that stands and hits did so on 98% of the chases and all the hops, the spacer on 74% of the chases, the timer on all of them.

    • edgeCritRule

      public boolean edgeCritRule
      The crit in (JumpIn.EDGE): at an opponent standing still on the ground, a running jump timed to come down into its reach late in the fall, and the critical hit as it does. Since 22 October, from the fight traces: against the one that stands and hits, every exchange was a hit for a hit (16.6 trades a fight, 0.3 crits of its own).

    • aimLevel

      public boolean aimLevel
      The aim rule (AimRule) brings the camera level with the fighter's own eye on the opponent (where its body spans that height) instead of onto the middle of it: the shortest ray to it, so the most reach. Since 22 October.

    • edgeHoldRule

      public boolean edgeHoldRule
      Spacing in: with the opponent just out of reach and its sword ready, it does not walk into that reach but stands at the edge and lets the opponent come, going in once that sword has been spent (or after a second of waiting); see EdgeHold. Since 19 October, on trial in training.

    • selfCritShare

      public float selfCritShare
      In self-play, the share of the scripted fights that goes to the stage with the opponents it still loses to (the crit stage and its kinds: spacer, timer, jumper, punisher...). The rest is shared by the earlier stages, whose opponents it beats four rounds in five. 0.5 up to 19 October.

    • watchStyles

      public boolean watchStyles
      In /swordai fight, how the opponent fights is counted and kept in swordai/people/<name>.json (a few hundred bytes a player), and training fights scripted opponents made from those it has lost to or nearly; see PersonStyle and StageSpec.peopleShare.

    • aimRule

      public boolean aimRule
      In the ticks after it has been hit, until it has hit back, the camera is brought onto the opponent for it; see AimRule.

    • backRule

      public boolean backRule
      In the twelve ticks after each hit of a combo it is taking (from the second hit in a row), S is held for it: it backs out, and comes in again for the first hit. A rule, from the stage on that keeps the push for S for good (StageSpec.backNudgeKeep), in training and in every fight. It is what the push at its full strength came to anyway (S on 94 to 98 ticks in 100 of those), said outright, and nothing the network learns can wear it down. False leaves it to the push.

    • jumpResetChance

      public float jumpResetChance
      The share of the hits of a combo it is taking (the second in a row and every later one) that it jumps with, W and the sprint key down, on the tick it learns of the hit: a jump reset, which halves how far the hit throws it, so that it comes down with the opponent in its reach and a swing to make; see JumpReset. On the rest, and on a hit that finds it in the air, S is held as backRule has it. Never on the first hit. 0: never, which is how it was up to the first evening against people, when backing off with S was all it did about a combo and a player who came after it with a running jump and a critical hit had it for as long as he liked.

    • comboStrafeRule

      public boolean comboStrafeRule
      From the second hit of a combo it is taking, A or D held for half a second after each such hit, away from the way the opponent is moving across its view: out of the line the combo comes down, and in again from the side; see ComboStrafe. With jumpResetChance it is a jump out to the side. The user, 23 October: it "don't know how to run and run to left or right to make its combo hard to continue and go back in". Off until measured.

    • jumpResetCounterChance

      public float jumpResetCounterChance
      The share of the hits that find it with its sword still on the way back from a hit of its own (no more than thirteen ticks after it) that it jumps with as well: the opponent's answer to its hit, which it has no swing to answer; see JumpReset. 0: only ever in a combo.

      Off. Measured with the network not learning: in a fast exchange nearly every hit it takes comes within those thirteen ticks, so it jumped with nine hits in ten (64 jumps a minute against the opponent that follows its hits with a running jump, 84 against the one that answers every hit), which is far more of this than was asked for; it then landed 69 hits to 73 taken against the first, where it is 55 to 68 without, and no better than before against the second, and its sweeps went from one hit in twelve to one in six.

    • jumpResetChasers

      public boolean jumpResetChasers
      Against an opponent that has followed a hit with a second one made from the air in the last twenty seconds (the running jump and the critical hit), the first hit is jumped with as well; see JumpReset. False: only ever from the second hit in a row, against anyone.

      Off. Tried for ten minutes of training: every opponent that makes critical hits counts as one of those, so it jumped with nearly every hit it took (77 jumps a minute against the one this was meant for, where it had been 20), which is the fighter nobody can combo that this was not to become; and it gained nothing by it (62 hits landed to 78 taken, for 54 to 68), while the hits it then made from a standstill were sweeps, three in ten.

    • stepBackRule

      public boolean stepBackRule
      Against an opponent that answers its hits while its sword is on the way back (twice within five seconds), it walks backwards out of that opponent's reach after each hit of its own until its sword is nearly back; see StepBack. What it keeps clear of is the critical hit such an opponent makes on its way down, which there is no swing to answer with.

      Off since the evening of 14 October. Against the scripted opponents it took fewer hits for as many landed; against people it was the S habit again in another place: after its own hit it walked backwards, an opponent who came straight on had the first hit, and what the user saw was a fighter that hardly combos and loses to weak players. In fifteen fights against six players it took 47 hits a minute where it had been taking 39, and landed 51 for 47.

    • chaseInCombo

      public boolean chaseInCombo
      The chase jump (chaseRule) is also the next hit of a combo of its own, at an opponent that backs off after being hit; see JumpIn.chaseInCombo.

    • meetJumpRule

      public boolean meetJumpRule
      An opponent that is coming at it through the air, still on its way up, is run at and hit the moment it is under the crosshair, if the sword is back; see MeetJump. A critical hit is only made on the way down, and this is the hit that gets there first.

    • selfPlayTurns

      public boolean selfPlayTurns
      Against a copy of itself, who makes its move first is drawn on every tick. Up to the first runs of 0.14.0 the copy always moved first and the fighter after it, and that alone decided most fights between equals; see EpisodePlan.mixedTurns. False is that.

    • screenCopyLagTicks

      public int screenCopyLagTicks
      Training on the screen against a copy of itself: the copy sees the fighter this many ticks later than it otherwise would. The user's character sees the copy a tick late and its clicks reach the server a tick late, as a player's do; the copy plays on the server and has neither delay, and without this the fight is one against an opponent that is always two ticks ahead (0.4 to 0.6 hits landed for each taken, against a copy it is level with off the screen).

    • fightRolloutSteps

      public int fightRolloutSteps
      A fight against a real opponent is learned from this many steps at a time (20 a second), far fewer than a training stage gathers: such fights are short and each of them is worth more.

    • fightAutoRespawn

      public boolean fightAutoRespawn
      /swordai fight: respawn by itself after dying, so a series of fights needs no hands.

    • sparCountdownTicks

      public int sparCountdownTicks
      /swordai spar: ticks of stand-off before each round.

    • rehearsalProbability

      public float rehearsalProbability
      Probability that an episode replays an earlier stage, so old skills keep being practised.
